content: Postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV) is a frequent complication that occurs after general anesthesia. It is associated with patient dissatisfaction, increased healthcare costs, and, in some cases, unplanned hospital admissions. Administering additional intravenous crystalloids during the perioperative period has been proposed as a simple and effective strategy to prevent PONV. The objective of this review was to evaluate whether supplemental intravenous crystalloid administration can prevent PONV in patients undergoing surgical procedures under general anesthesia. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and CINAHL, up to August 2018. Additional searches included clinical trial registries, conference proceedings, and citation tracking. The review included randomized controlled trials involving patients older than six months who received supplemental perioperative intravenous crystalloids in volumes greater than those given to comparator groups. A total of 41 studies, encompassing 4224 participants, were included in the analysis. Most participants underwent ambulatory or short-stay surgical procedures and were classified as American Society of Anesthesiology (ASA) class I or II. The studies were conducted in diverse geographic locations and surgical centers. However, the risk of bias was generally unclear across the included studies. The findings suggest that supplemental intravenous crystalloid administration likely reduces the overall risk of postoperative nausea (PON) with a risk ratio (RR) of 0.62 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.51 to 0.75) based on moderate-certainty evidence from 18 studies involving 1766 participants. When analyzed by time, the intervention reduced the risk of early PON (within the first six hours postoperatively) with an RR of 0.67 (95% CI 0.58 to 0.78; 20 studies; 2310 participants) and late PON (up to or including 24 hours postoperatively) with an RR of 0.47 (95% CI 0.32 to 0.69; 17 studies; 1682 participants). Similarly, supplemental intravenous crystalloids likely reduce the risk of postoperative vomiting (POV) with an RR of 0.50 (95% CI 0.40 to 0.63; 20 studies; 1970 participants). This effect was observed for both early POV (RR 0.56, 95% CI 0.41 to 0.76; 19 studies; 1998 participants) and late POV (RR 0.48, 95% CI 0.29 to 0.79; 15 studies; 1403 participants), based on moderate-certainty evidence. The intervention also likely reduces the need for pharmacologic treatment of PONV, with an RR of 0.62 (95% CI 0.51 to 0.76; 23 studies; 2416 participants). However, its effect on the risk of unplanned postoperative hospital admission remains unclear, with an RR of 1.05 (95% CI 0.77 to 1.43; 3 studies; 235 participants), based on low-certainty evidence. No studies reported serious adverse events, such as admission to a high-dependency unit, postoperative cardiac or respiratory complications, or death, associated with supplemental perioperative intravenous crystalloid administration. In conclusion, there is moderate-certainty evidence that supplemental perioperative intravenous crystalloid administration reduces the risk of PON and POV in ASA class I to II patients undergoing ambulatory or short-stay surgical procedures under general anesthesia. The intervention also likely reduces the need for pharmacologic treatment of PONV. However, its impact on unplanned postoperative hospital admissions and the risk of serious adverse events remains uncertain. Further research, including the assessment of one study awaiting classification, may influence these conclusions.
